title: People Essential for Biodiversity in Rural Japan — Study
paragraphs: Have you ever thought about what the world would be like if humans just ... disappeared? You might imagine that nature would make a dramatic comeback, with more insects and birds, wild animals, plants and trees.
However, a study from Japan has found that humans may actually be essential for maintaining biodiversity in some rural areas.

Japan is experiencing severe depopulation in its rural areas as people increasingly move into urban centers. Twenty-three of Japan's 47 prefectures have been depopulating since 1995, while many remote areas have seen population decreases since the 1950s.
A team of researchers from Japan and the UK wanted to see what effects depopulation actually has on biodiversity.

Using data collected by citizen scientists for a nationwide biodiversity monitoring project, the researchers analyzed changes among 464 species of animals, as well as over 2,900 plant species. The data was collected in areas such as woods, farms, rural towns and villages across Japan over periods of between five and 17 years from 2004.

The findings showed that biodiversity decreased irrespective of whether the human population in an area increased or decreased. However, in areas where human populations were stable, biodiversity was also stable.
The study authors explained that biodiversity has become dependent on people in Japan's rural areas because they have been managing the land there for thousands of years.

Living on small-scale farms in the spaces between steep, forested mountains and more densely populated urban centers, people have cultivated diverse landscapes of rice paddies, ponds, orchards, grassland and woodland. Many of the plants and animals in these semi-natural ecosystems now depend on people to maintain these landscapes.
According to the authors, Japan is a forerunner for understanding how depopulation is likely to affect biodiversity in other places around the world with similar semi-natural ecosystems.

They say that maintaining wildlife-friendly farming practices in semi-natural landscapes is essential in areas facing depopulation, and all countries with decreasing populations must consider its impacts on conservation.
